title: Best AML Software for Banks in 2026
summary: AML software for banks compared by size and job: human sign-off, audit trails and exam evidence across Sphinx, Verafin, Actimize, Oracle, SAS and more.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** The best AML software for banks depends on the size of the bank and on where the work is stuck. Monitoring systems such as Nasdaq Verafin, NICE Actimize and Oracle generate and manage alerts, while Sphinx sits on top of them and does the investigation work, with the bank's team keeping final approval. At a $30B+ US bank, Sphinx recorded a 94% false-positive reduction and 98.8% agreement with the BSA officer.


Sphinx wrote this list and appears on it. The vendors were chosen because they are sold to banks today and their products could be checked against published material, and the numbering is an order of fit for a US bank already running a monitoring system, not a quality score.


This post is narrower than Sphinx's[full AML software comparison](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/best-aml-software) , which also covers fintech and crypto tools. Banks in the $1B to $10B range should also read the guide to[AML technology for community banks](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/aml-compliance-solutions-for-community-banks) , which goes deeper on core integration and cost per alert.


## Start with who signs, what's on record, and what an examiner can test


Bank compliance software gets judged on three questions before anyone looks at a feature list. Who makes the final call, can the reasoning be reconstructed later, and what will an examiner or independent tester be able to review?


The[FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual](https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/manual/AssessingComplianceWithBSARegulatoryRequirements/04) answers the first two directly. The decision maker, whether a person or a committee, should have authority over the final SAR filing decision, and banks should document the specific reason for filing or not filing. The same section says a monitoring system's programming methodology and effectiveness should be independently validated. That validation sits alongside the broader independent testing of alert management and SAR decisions.


Any tool that touches an alert has to fit inside that structure. Ask each vendor where the human decision happens, and what record it leaves when an alert gets closed rather than escalated.


## How SR 26-2 changes the model risk conversation


[SR 26-2](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.htm) , issued in April 2026, replaced SR 11-7 and the 2021 BSA/AML model risk statement, SR 21-8. The letter says it is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets. OCC Bulletin 2026-13 adds that smaller banks may still find it relevant if they have significant model exposure.


Three details matter for an AML purchase. Deterministic rule-based processes fall outside the guidance's definition of a model, while statistical and non-generative machine learning models fall inside it. Generative and agentic AI models are out of scope entirely, under footnote 3, which leaves the bank's own risk management and governance to determine the controls. And the OCC states the guidance sets no enforceable standards, though the guidance also notes that supervisory action may still follow violations of law or unsafe practices.


So no agentic AI product on this list, Sphinx included, can claim to satisfy SR 26-2. Your institution's governance covers those agents, and the agencies have said a request for information on bank AI use is planned. The post on[AML model validation](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/aml-model-validation-requirements) covers the detection side in more detail.


Program rules are moving too. FinCEN's[April 2026 proposal](https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-proposes-rule-fundamentally-reform-financial-institution-programs) would focus AML/CFT programs on effectiveness. Check its status when you read this, because current requirements apply until a final rule takes effect.

## The investigation layer


### 1. Sphinx: best for the investigation work on top of the bank's monitoring system


Sphinx provides AI compliance analysts, not a monitoring system. Its agents log into the tools a team already uses, then review alerts, gather evidence and write case notes. Sphinx prepares the evidence, applies your SOPs, and produces a traceable recommendation; your team retains final approval. It sits on top of tools like Verafin or Actimize rather than replacing them, and each step is logged through an[interpretable framework](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-sphinx-makes-every-decision-auditable---the-interpretable-agentic-framework) .


It suits banks whose detection works but whose investigators can't keep pace. Beyond the $30B+ bank result above, Sphinx reports 0 audit findings involving Sphinx-handled cases and a 13-day median to live. That is an audit figure, not a promise about any exam. Sia Partners independently validated the KYC, KYB and TM agents.


The limit comes from what it is. Sphinx generates no alerts, so a bank without a monitoring system needs one first, and its governance team has to own how the agents are overseen.


## A system spanning a wide range of bank sizes


### 2. Nasdaq Verafin: best for fraud and AML on one cloud platform


Nasdaq Verafin combines fraud detection, AML monitoring, case management, due diligence and SAR and CTR filing in one cloud platform, drawing on a consortium Nasdaq puts at more than 2,800 customers. Its Agentic AI Workforce adds role-based analysts for sanctions, EDD, AML and fraud, and Nasdaq says more than 650 institutions use it.


It suits institutions that want fraud and AML in one place and value cross-institution data. Testimonials on its agentic page run from a $500M credit union to a $35B bank.


The limit is coverage of newer agents. Its June 2026 announcement said the AML analyst would start with cash structuring alerts, with other typologies to follow, and described third-party overlay as entering beta. Auto-dispositioning is also configurable, so each bank has to decide where human review stays mandatory.


## Suites aimed at larger and global banks


### 3. NICE Actimize: best for enterprise programs that want one suite


Actimize covers Suspicious Activity Monitoring, KYC, sanctions screening, entity risk and regulatory reporting, with rules and machine learning layered in SAM. Agentic AI is embedded in ActOne workflows to gather context and draft SAR narratives. Actimize's brochure keeps final decisions with investigators, who review and approve filings.


It suits large banks running broad programs; NICE's CFO has pointed to renewals with top-tier institutions. AML Essentials packages core coverage for regional and community banks.


The limit comes with a suite this broad: it is a long-term platform commitment, which makes ownership worth checking.[CTech reported in September 2026](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/iazqvedg2) that Brookfield was in exclusive talks to buy Actimize from NICE, with no finalized deal. Buyers should ask how a change of owner would affect contracts, support and roadmap.


### 4. Oracle Financial Crime and Compliance Management: best for multi-jurisdiction programs


Oracle FCCM is an end-to-end SaaS suite covering transaction monitoring, customer screening, KYC, an Investigation Hub and regulatory reporting. Its AI Investigator helps analysts summarize activity and draft SAR narratives inside human-in-the-loop workflows, and governance controls include versioning, approvals, rollback and lineage.


Oracle describes the suite as tailored for global banks and financial institutions, so it suits programs that need common controls across business lines and jurisdictions.


The limit follows from that breadth. The suite runs on Oracle's unified data model and pipelines, so customer, account and transaction data have to be loaded and maintained there. Treat it as a data program as well as a software purchase.


### 5. SAS Anti-Money Laundering: best for banks that want to inspect and customize models


SAS combines transaction monitoring, machine learning, customer due diligence, entity resolution, investigation management and reporting on SAS Viya. Its materials describe a white-box approach to machine learning, with model governance and network analytics for finding hidden relationships.


It suits banks with analytics staff who want to examine and adjust detection logic themselves. The product page doesn't segment by asset size, so this list places it here based on that operating model rather than a stated customer band.


The limit is the other side of that control. Models a bank customizes are models the bank has to document and validate, and at larger banks statistical and machine learning models sit within SR 26-2's definition. Budget model risk staff time alongside the license.


## Systems built for community and regional banks


### 6. Abrigo BAM+: best for community programs that tune their own scenarios


BAM+ unifies monitoring, investigations and regulatory filing, using configurable rules, behavioral analysis and machine learning scenarios. An optional AML Assistant scores alerts and shows the factors behind each score. Scenario Tuner supports above-the-line and below-the-line testing, and SARs and CTRs file directly to FinCEN.


Abrigo says it built the product for community banks and credit unions, and the ICBA lists it among its BSA solutions. It suits small teams that want tuning evidence ready for examiners.


The limit is that alert scoring ranks the queue and gives an AI-generated starting point, while analysts still work the review. Banks with cross-border or multi-entity programs should test fit, given the community focus.


### 7. Jack Henry Financial Crimes Defender: best for Jack Henry core banks combining fraud and BSA work


Defender is a cloud-native fraud and AML platform that monitors transactions, gathers case documents, screens against OFAC and other watchlists, and generates SARs and CTRs. An open API connects custom cores and third-party systems.


Jack Henry aims it at community and regional institutions, and the ICBA lists it too. It suits banks that want fraud and BSA teams working from one window.


The limit is core availability. Jack Henry's product page lists general availability for SilverLake, an early adopter phase for Symitar, and integrations for CIF 20/20 and Core Director as upcoming, so confirm current status for your core. Real-time decisioning also depends on Defender receiving the transaction in real time.


## Questions that separate these options


Six questions will narrow this list without a demo.


1. Is your problem detection or investigation? Weak coverage calls for a monitoring change, and a backlog on sound alerts calls for investigation capacity on top.
2. Who closes a false positive? Get the answer per alert type, and check that it matches your written procedures.
3. Can a tester rebuild one closed alert from the record alone, including the data reviewed, the procedure applied and the person who approved it?
4. How would each component classify under SR 26-2: deterministic rule, statistical model, or agentic AI outside the guidance? Then ask who in your bank governs each one.
5. What proof comes from a bank of your size, and is it an audit result, a pilot metric or a vendor estimate?
6. What would a change of owner, or a move to another core, do to your contract and roadmap?


The guide to[BSA exam preparation](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/community-bank-bsa-exam-preparation) shows where those answers land when examiners arrive. The examiner is reviewing your program, and no vendor can carry that for you.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can AI software make the final SAR decision at a bank?


The FFIEC manual expects a decision maker, an individual or a committee, with authority over the final SAR filing decision, plus documentation of why the bank did or did not file. Sphinx prepares the evidence and a traceable recommendation, and your team retains final approval. Confirm the same arrangement in writing with any vendor.


### Does SR 26-2 apply to AI agents used in AML investigations?


Footnote 3 of the guidance puts generative and agentic AI models out of scope and points banks to their own risk management and governance practices. Vendors therefore can't claim their agents satisfy SR 26-2. Statistical and non-generative machine learning models in a detection system remain within the guidance, which is expected to be most relevant above $30 billion in assets.


### Can we keep Verafin or Actimize and add an AI investigation layer?


Yes. Sphinx sits on top of tools like Verafin or Actimize and works in the systems analysts already use, so the monitoring system stays in place. Both vendors also sell agentic features of their own, so compare typology coverage, human review settings and audit records before deciding which layer does the work.


### What AML software do community banks use compared with large banks?


Published material points community banks toward Abrigo BAM+, Jack Henry Financial Crimes Defender and Nasdaq Verafin, and toward Actimize's AML Essentials package. Oracle describes its suite as tailored for global banks, and NICE has reported Actimize renewals among top-tier institutions. Asset size is a starting point, because product complexity and cross-border activity can matter more.


### How much does AML software cost for a bank?


None of the monitoring vendors above list a price on the product pages reviewed for this list, so expect a scoped quote; Oracle describes pay-per-use subscription pricing for its cloud service. Sphinx is priced as a platform fee plus usage tiers scoped to your volumes. Include data work, validation and tuning time when you compare quotes.
